rw: Assets conventionally sit in the 1000 series of a chart of accounts, with liabilities in 2000, equity in 3000, revenue in 4000 and expenses in 5000.

ww.The 5000 series: The 5000 series is normally reserved for expenses such as rent and wages, not for assets, which are numbered in the 1000 range.
ww.The 4000 series: The 4000 series usually holds revenue accounts such as sales and service fees, which increase equity rather than represent items the business owns.
ww.The 3000 series: The 3000 series is conventionally used for owner's equity accounts such as capital and drawings, not for the resources a business owns.

rw: Straight-line depreciation is (cost minus salvage) divided by useful life: ($24,000 - $0) / 4 years = $6,000 of expense each year, spread evenly over the van's life.

ww.$96,000: $96,000 multiplies the cost by the 4-year life instead of dividing, which is the wrong operation and gives an amount far above the van's price.
ww.$4,000: $4,000 would result from dividing the cost by 6 rather than by the 4-year life, so it does not match straight-line depreciation here.
ww.$24,000: $24,000 is the full cost of the van, which would be expensed all at once; depreciation spreads that cost over the four years of use.

rw: Straight-line rate is 1/5 = 20%, doubled to 40%; applied to the full $20,000 book value (salvage ignored), year-one depreciation is $20,000 x 40% = $8,000.

ww.$4,000: $4,000 is the straight-line amount ($20,000 / 5 years); double-declining-balance uses twice the straight-line rate, so first-year expense must be larger than this.
ww.$20,000: $20,000 is the entire cost of the asset, which would be written off in one year; depreciation only allocates a fraction of cost each year.
ww.$2,000: $2,000 would come from applying only 10% to the cost, half the straight-line rate, instead of doubling the 20% rate to 40%.

rw: Accumulated depreciation is a contra-asset account that adds up all depreciation expense recorded on an asset since purchase; subtracting it from cost gives book value.

ww.The yearly expense only, shown on the in: The yearly expense on the income statement is depreciation expense; accumulated depreciation is the running total of all years on the balance sheet.
ww.The resale price of the asset when sold: Resale price is market value, which can differ from book value; accumulated depreciation is an accounting allocation of cost, not an estimate of what the asset would sell for.
ww.The cost of the asset when it was first: The original purchase price is the asset's historical cost; accumulated depreciation is the portion of that cost already written off, not the cost itself.

rw: Book value equals cost minus accumulated depreciation: $15,000 - $9,000 = $6,000, the portion of the asset's cost not yet expensed.

ww.$15,000: $15,000 is the original cost; book value is cost minus accumulated depreciation, so it must be lower once depreciation has been recorded.
ww.$24,000: $24,000 adds the accumulated depreciation to the cost, but accumulated depreciation is subtracted from cost to find book value, never added.
ww.$9,000: $9,000 is only the accumulated depreciation; book value is what remains after subtracting it from the $15,000 cost.

rw: Revenue is earned evenly: $3,600 / 12 months = $300 per month, and 3 months x $300 = $900 earned, leaving $2,700 as unearned revenue.

ww.$3,600: $3,600 is the whole contract amount; only a portion is earned after 3 months, and the rest remains unearned revenue, a liability until services are performed.
ww.$1,200: $1,200 would be four months of service ($300 x 4) or a third of the contract; only 3 of 12 months have passed, so the fraction is one quarter.
ww.$300: $300 is the revenue for just one month; three months have passed, so earned revenue is $300 x 3 = $900.

rw: Closing entries zero out temporary accounts (revenue, expenses, drawings) and transfer the net result to owner's equity, so the next period starts with fresh balances.

ww.Increase revenue by recording extra sale: Closing entries record no new sales; they only transfer balances already recorded, and inventing revenue would be fraud rather than an accounting procedure.
ww.Cancel the business and send all the sta: Closing entries are a bookkeeping step at the end of a period; they have nothing to do with ending the business or dismissing employees.
ww.Delete all assets from the books so that: Closing entries never remove assets; permanent accounts like assets, liabilities and capital carry their balances forward into the next accounting period.

rw: Income Summary collects revenues (credits) and expenses (debits); a $14,000 credit balance means revenues exceeded expenses, so net income of $14,000 transfers to capital.

ww.Drawings of $14,000: Drawings are a debit-balance owner withdrawal account closed to capital; a credit balance in Income Summary instead reflects revenues exceeding expenses.
ww.Net loss of $14,000: A net loss shows as a debit balance in Income Summary because expenses exceed revenues; a credit balance signals the opposite result.
ww.Total assets of $14,000: Total assets are a balance sheet item and are not measured in Income Summary, which is a temporary account used only to compute profit or loss.

rw: A subsidiary ledger holds detailed accounts, such as individual customers or vendors, whose total must equal the related control account in the general ledger.

ww.A ledger kept by a rival firm to check t: A rival firm's records have nothing to do with the business's own books; a subsidiary ledger is an internal detail ledger supporting a control account.
ww.A ledger with no entries in it, kept by: A subsidiary ledger is full of detailed entries, one account per customer or vendor, so describing it as empty misses its entire purpose.
ww.A tax calendar that shows the filing dat: A tax calendar is a scheduling tool for filing deadlines, not a ledger; it holds no debit or credit account balances at all.

rw: The $300 gap (18,500 - 18,200) signals a posting or addition error somewhere; the accountant should trace entries to find and correct it so both agree.

ww.Ignore the difference and close the book: Ignoring a difference between the control account and subsidiary total leaves an error uncorrected, which undermines the reliability of the receivables balance.
ww.Adjust revenue by $300 at once, so the a: Adjusting revenue merely to make accounts agree would hide the true error and could misstate income; the actual mistake has to be found and fixed.
ww.Delete the subsidiary ledger and start a: Deleting the subsidiary ledger would destroy the customer detail needed to collect payments; a $300 variance is fixed by investigation, not by discarding records.

rw: Collecting on account increases Cash (debit) and decreases Accounts Receivable (credit); revenue was already recorded when the sale was made on credit.

ww.Debit Revenue $500 and credit Cash $500: This entry reverses the effect: it credits cash and debits revenue, but collecting a receivable brings cash in and does not involve revenue at all.
ww.Debit Cash $500 and credit Revenue $500: Crediting Revenue would count the sale twice, since revenue was recognized at the time of the credit sale; collection only converts the receivable into cash.
ww.Debit Accounts Receivable $500; credit C: This reverses the real entry: it would increase receivables and reduce cash, which is what happens when granting credit, not collecting from a customer.

rw: The policy runs April 1 to March 31, so 9 months have passed by December 31: $1,200 / 12 = $100 per month x 9 = $900 insurance expense.

ww.$1,200: $1,200 is the full annual premium; only 9 of the 12 months have elapsed by December 31, so the remaining 3 months stay as prepaid insurance.
ww.$300: $300 is the portion left unexpired (3 months x $100) at December 31, which remains in Prepaid Insurance rather than being expensed.
ww.$100: $100 is the cost of just one month of coverage; nine months from April through December have been used up.

rw: Interest = principal x rate x time: $5,000 x 0.06 x (90/360) = $5,000 x 0.06 x 0.25 = $75 earned over the 90 days.

ww.$750: $750 would result from using 10 percent for a full year or a longer time; the 6 percent rate over 90 days produces much less interest.
ww.$7.50: $7.50 is off by a factor of ten, likely a misplaced decimal when applying 6% and 90/360 to the $5,000 principal.
ww.$300: $300 is the interest for a full year (5,000 x 6%); the note is only held for 90 days, a quarter of a year, so interest is smaller.

rw: NSF stands for non-sufficient funds: the drawer's balance was too low to cover the check, so the bank returns it and the seller must collect another way.

ww.The check was a gift from the customer t: A returned check is not a gift; it is a failed payment, so the customer still owes the seller the amount of the check.
ww.The check was paid in full by the bank t: NSF means the opposite of being paid in full: the bank refused payment because funds were lacking, so the seller has not been paid.
ww.The check was approved twice by the bank: Banks pay a check only once; NSF means it bounced and was returned unpaid, and nothing was paid even one time.

rw: Trade discount is 20% x $800 = $160, so the invoice price is $800 - $160 = $640, the amount the buyer actually owes before any cash discount.

ww.$160: $160 is the discount amount itself (20% of $800), not the price; the invoice price is the list price minus that discount.
ww.$960: $960 adds the discount to the list price instead of subtracting it; a trade discount lowers what the buyer pays.
ww.$780: $780 subtracts only $20, as if the discount were a flat dollar amount; a 20% trade discount takes off $160 from the $800 list price.

rw: Freight-in is the transportation cost the buyer pays to get purchased goods delivered, and it is added to the cost of inventory purchased.

ww.A discount for early payment of the invo: A discount for early payment is a purchase or cash discount, which lowers what the buyer pays; freight-in is a delivery cost that adds to cost.
ww.A tax on imports charged at the border b: An import tax charged at the border is a customs duty or tariff, a different cost from the transportation charge called freight-in.
ww.Shipping paid by the seller to customers: Shipping the seller pays to deliver goods to customers is freight-out, a selling expense of the seller, not freight-in.

rw: Freight-in is part of inventory cost: $5,000 purchase price + $400 freight = $5,400 total cost of the goods bought.

ww.$400: $400 is only the freight; total cost of goods includes both the purchase price and the transportation paid by the buyer to receive them.
ww.$4,600: $4,600 subtracts the freight from the price, but freight-in is added to the cost of the goods, not deducted from it.
ww.$5,000: $5,000 leaves out the $400 freight; the buyer's cost of goods includes the shipping needed to bring the goods to its location.

rw: A credit purchase creates a liability to the supplier, so Accounts Payable increases with a credit while Inventory or Purchases is debited.

ww.Accounts Receivable: Accounts Receivable is an asset for money owed by customers; buying from a supplier creates an amount the business owes, not one it is owed.
ww.Owner's Capital: Owner's Capital changes with investments, profits and drawings; a purchase on credit from a supplier does not directly change the owner's investment.
ww.Cash account: Cash would be affected only if the purchase were paid immediately; a credit purchase delays payment, so the liability rises while cash stays unchanged.

rw: A cash discount, such as 2/10 n/30, is a reduction offered for paying an invoice early, which gives the supplier faster access to its money.

ww.A trade discount from the price list of: A trade discount reduces the list price before the invoice is prepared; a cash discount is a separate reduction offered for prompt payment of the invoice.
ww.A late fee charged when an invoice is pa: A charge added for paying after the due date is a late fee or finance charge, the opposite of a discount for paying early.
ww.A tax added to the invoice by the state: A tax added by the state is a sales tax collected for government; it is not a reduction the supplier offers to speed up payment.

rw: Day 12 is within the 15-day discount period, so the buyer takes 1% of $2,500 = $25 off and pays $2,500 - $25 = $2,475.

ww.$2,525: $2,525 adds 1% to the invoice, but a discount reduces the amount paid; the buyer who pays early owes less than the invoice total.
ww.$2,250: $2,250 takes off 10% rather than 1%; the terms 1/15 allow only a 1% discount ($25) when paid within 15 days.
ww.$2,500: $2,500 is the full invoice amount; the terms 1/15 let the buyer subtract 1% for paying within 15 days, and day 12 qualifies.

rw: The liabilities section of the balance sheet lists amounts the business owes to creditors, such as accounts payable, notes payable and accrued expenses.

ww.Owner equity: Owner's equity shows the owner's claim on the business (assets minus liabilities), not amounts owed to outside creditors.
ww.Revenue: Revenue appears on the income statement, not the balance sheet, and it describes earnings rather than debts owed to others.
ww.Asset list: Assets list what the business owns, such as cash and equipment; the debts owed to creditors appear on the other side of the equation as liabilities.

rw: Debt ratio = total liabilities / total assets = $60,000 / $150,000 = 0.40 = 40%, meaning creditors fund 40 cents of each asset dollar.

ww.250%: 250% inverts the fraction (150,000 / 60,000); the debt ratio puts liabilities in the numerator over assets in the denominator, so it cannot exceed 100% here.
ww.90%: 90% is not what the data produce; $60,000 of liabilities is well below $150,000 of assets, so most assets are not financed by debt.
ww.60%: 60% uses the liabilities figure ($60,000) as a percent, but the ratio must divide liabilities by assets before converting to percent.

rw: Ending retained earnings = beginning + net income - dividends = $40,000 + $25,000 - $5,000 = $60,000, the profit kept in the business.

ww.$20,000: $20,000 subtracts earnings from the starting balance; retained earnings grow by net income and shrink by dividends, so it should not drop that far.
ww.$70,000: $70,000 adds the $25,000 income but then ignores the $5,000 dividends, which reduce retained earnings when paid out to shareholders.
ww.$65,000: $65,000 equals the beginning balance plus income minus nothing else, but it fails to subtract dividends correctly: 40,000 + 25,000 = 65,000 less 5,000 still must be applied.

rw: A comparative statement presents figures for two or more periods side by side, so readers can see changes and trends in sales, expenses and assets.

ww.A statement with no numbers, only words: A statement with only words and no numbers is not a financial statement; comparative statements are numeric and show multiple periods together.
ww.A statement comparing the owner to the w: Comparative statements compare financial results over time, not the pay and hours of owners and employees, which is a labor matter.
ww.A statement printed in color on glossy p: Color and glossy paper are matters of presentation; what makes a statement comparative is multi-period data, not how it is printed.

ww.1.5%: 1.5% results from misplacing the decimal point; the change of $60,000 on a base of $400,000 gives a much larger percent increase.
ww.13%: 13% divides the $60,000 increase by the new figure ($460,000) instead of the earlier year's $400,000; the base must be the prior period.
ww.60%: 60% treats the $60,000 dollar change as a percent; it must be divided by the $400,000 starting sales amount to get 15%.

rw: Horizontal analysis compares the same line item across several periods, showing dollar and percent changes, which reveals trends over time.

ww.Only cash items in the books of a firm: Horizontal analysis is not limited to cash items; it can be applied to any line of a statement across periods.
ww.Items within one period as percentages: Expressing items within one period as percentages of a base is vertical (common-size) analysis, not horizontal analysis.
ww.Different companies only, in one year: Comparing different companies in one year is cross-company benchmarking; horizontal analysis follows one company's items through time.

rw: Vertical analysis expresses each item as a percent of a base, such as net sales on the income statement or total assets on the balance sheet.

ww.Compare one item over many years, as it: Comparing one item over many years is horizontal (trend) analysis; vertical analysis looks within a single period instead.
ww.Remove expenses from the income statemen: Vertical analysis removes nothing from the statements; it keeps all expenses and restates each as a percentage of a base amount.
ww.Print statements vertically on the page: Vertical has nothing to do with page orientation; it refers to analyzing each item as a percent of a base within one statement.

rw: COGS % of sales = $120,000 / $300,000 = 0.40 = 40%, so 40 cents of each sales dollar goes to the cost of the goods sold.

ww.60%: 60% is the remainder, the gross profit margin ($180,000 / $300,000); the question asks for cost of goods sold as a percent of sales.
ww.12%: 12% results from a decimal slip; $120,000 divided by $300,000 is 0.40, not 0.12.
ww.250%: 250% flips the fraction ($300,000 / $120,000); the cost of goods sold must be the numerator over net sales to get a percent of sales.

rw: Earnings per share = net income / shares outstanding = $360,000 / 120,000 = $3.00 earned for each share held.

ww.$30.00: $30.00 is off by a factor of ten; $360,000 divided by 120,000 shares is $3.00, not $30.00 per share.
ww.$0.33: $0.33 flips the division (120,000 / 360,000); EPS puts earnings in the numerator and shares outstanding in the denominator.
ww.$240,000: $240,000 is the difference between earnings and shares (360,000 - 120,000), a meaningless subtraction; EPS is a per-share ratio found by dividing.

rw: Lenders review income, cash flow, assets and debts to judge whether the company can repay a loan with interest on time.

ww.To set its advertising plans each year: Advertising plans are set by the company's managers and marketing staff; lenders read statements to judge credit risk, not to plan promotions.
ww.To choose its logo and its colors: A company's logo and colors are branding choices unrelated to its finances; lenders want evidence that debts will be repaid.
ww.To count its employees and its offices: Headcount and office locations are operating details; lenders focus on profitability, liquidity and leverage reported in the financial statements.

rw: Notes to the financial statements explain accounting methods, assumptions and contingencies and give details behind the numbers, which readers need to interpret statements fully.

ww.To replace the statements, so readers sk: Notes supplement the statements and cannot replace them; readers still need the balance sheet, income statement and cash flow figures.
ww.To advertise products to customers and t: Notes are about accounting disclosure and are not advertising; publicity for products belongs in marketing materials, not in audited statements.
ww.To hide losses from the owners and from: Notes exist to disclose information fully, not to conceal losses; hiding losses would violate full disclosure and may be fraud.

rw: When income is high but operating cash is negative, profits may be tied up in receivables or inventory, a sign of weak collections.

ww.Cash is guaranteed to grow in the coming: Negative operating cash flow does not guarantee future growth in cash; if anything, it signals a problem that needs management action.
ww.Net income is always wrong because the b: Net income is not always wrong; accrual accounting can legitimately differ from cash flow when revenue is earned but cash is not yet collected.
ww.The company has no customers and makes n: A company with strong net income clearly has customers and sales; the problem is converting those sales to cash, not an absence of sales.

rw: Consistency means using the same accounting methods from period to period so results are comparable, and any necessary change is disclosed in the notes.

ww.A business must hide changes in methods: The consistency principle requires methods to be applied the same way and changes disclosed, so concealing changes would violate it.
ww.A business must change methods each year: Changing methods every year would make statements incomparable; consistency requires stable methods unless a change is justified and explained.
ww.A business must use cash basis only and: Consistency does not restrict a company to cash basis; most businesses use accrual accounting, applied consistently each period.

rw: Changing inventory methods without disclosure breaks consistency (same methods over time) and full disclosure (telling readers about material changes affecting comparability).

ww.Time period assumption rule: The time period assumption splits operations into periods like months and years; switching inventory methods secretly is a different issue.
ww.Business entity, firm is separate: The business entity concept separates the owner's finances from the firm's; it does not concern changing inventory methods.
ww.Monetary unit assumption rule: The monetary unit assumption says transactions are measured in money; it does not address switching inventory costing methods.

rw: Conservatism says that when uncertain, accountants choose the option that does not overstate assets or income, such as lower of cost or market for inventory.

ww.Hide risks from the owners and the publi: Conservatism does not mean hiding risks; it means reporting uncertainty cautiously, not concealing facts from owners or the public.
ww.Never report losses in the statements, s: Conservatism does not prohibit reporting losses; probable losses should be recorded, not hidden so the firm looks profitable.
ww.Always report the highest profit possibl: Reporting the highest profit regardless of facts is the opposite of conservatism, which counsels caution about gains and anticipating possible losses.

rw: Hiding losses is unethical and may be illegal, so the accountant should refuse and use proper channels, such as the audit committee or compliance office.

ww.Hide it and tell nobody about the loss a: Concealing a loss is dishonest and misleads users of the statements; it could expose the accountant to legal and professional penalties.
ww.Comply to keep the job and avoid any arg: Complying to keep a job violates professional ethics; accountants must put honest reporting ahead of pressure from a manager.
ww.Alter the numbers slightly, so the loss: Altering numbers to shrink a loss is still falsifying records, which is fraud; the accountant should report the true figure.

rw: The IRS is the federal agency that collects income and other federal taxes and enforces the Internal Revenue Code through audits and penalties.

ww.Sets accounting standards and publishes: Setting accounting standards is the job of the FASB (and the SEC for public companies), not the IRS, which administers tax law.
ww.Regulates stock markets and company repo: Regulating stock markets and the reports of public companies is the job of the SEC, a separate agency from the IRS.
ww.Insures bank deposits up to a legal limi: Insuring bank deposits up to a legal limit is the role of the FDIC, not the IRS.

rw: The SEC requires public companies to file accurate and timely financial reports, such as 10-K and 10-Q forms, so investors can make informed decisions.

ww.Hires accountants for public companies t: Public companies hire their own accountants and auditors; the SEC does not keep their books but oversees what they disclose.
ww.Prints annual reports for the shareholde: The SEC does not print annual reports; companies prepare them and file required reports like the 10-K and 10-Q with the SEC.
ww.Sets sales prices for goods sold by publ: The SEC does not set sales prices; its role is investor protection and fair, orderly markets, not pricing of products.

rw: When one person orders, receives and approves payment, no one checks that person's work, which makes fraud and undetected errors easy; duties should be divided.

ww.One person orders and another pays, both: Having one person order and another pay, with a third reviewing, is separation of duties working properly, as it limits chances for fraud.
ww.Two people count cash together at the cl: Two people counting cash together is a dual control that supports separation of duties by letting each check the other.
ww.A manager reviews all payments made by t: A manager reviewing payments is an independent check, which strengthens internal control rather than violating separation of duties.

rw: An audit trail lets an auditor trace a transaction from the source document through journals and ledgers to the financial statements, or the reverse.

ww.A hiking path through the hills and wood: A hiking path has nothing to do with accounting; an audit trail is a documented sequence of records that lets reviewers follow transactions.
ww.A budget plan for the next year that the: A budget plan is a forecast of future income and spending, not a record of past transactions that can be traced back.
ww.A list of employees and the hours that t: A list of employees and hours is a payroll or time record; it may support an audit but is not itself the audit trail.

rw: Gross income is the total income from all sources before deductions or adjustments, and it is the starting point for computing taxable income.

ww.Only gifts received by a person in a yea: Gifts are only one possible item and are often excluded; gross income covers all income sources such as wages, interest and business earnings.
ww.Only wages earned from a regular job: Wages are just one source; gross income also includes interest, dividends, business profit and other income received during the year.
ww.Income left after all deductions apply: Income remaining after deductions is taxable income, not gross income, which is measured before any deductions are subtracted.

rw: Taxable income = gross income - deductions = $50,000 - $12,000 = $38,000, the amount to which tax rates are applied.

ww.$50,000: $50,000 is the gross income before the standard deduction is subtracted; taxable income is lower once the deduction is applied.
ww.$12,000: $12,000 is only the standard deduction; taxable income is what remains after subtracting it from gross income.
ww.$62,000: $62,000 adds the deduction to income, but deductions reduce taxable income and are never added to it.

rw: A progressive tax applies higher rates as income rises, so wealthier taxpayers pay a larger percentage, as in the US federal income tax brackets.

ww.Lower incomes pay higher rates than the: Lower incomes paying higher rates describes a regressive tax, the opposite of progressive.
ww.Everyone pays the same rate of tax on in: The same rate for everyone is a flat (proportional) tax, not a progressive system that raises rates with income.
ww.No one pays tax at all in the country: A system where nobody pays tax is not a tax system; progressive taxes raise revenue by taxing higher incomes at higher rates.

rw: A flat tax applies one single rate to every taxpayer's income, regardless of how much the person earns.

ww.A tax that rises as income moves higher: A tax that rises as income rises is a progressive tax; a flat tax holds the rate constant at all income levels.
ww.A tax only on sales of goods in shops: A tax only on sales is a sales tax, which is collected on purchases; a flat tax is an income tax with one rate.
ww.A tax on property such as land and homes: A tax on land and homes is a property tax; flat tax describes a single rate on income, not the type of asset taxed.

rw: Rent paid for office space is an ordinary and necessary cost of operating a business, so it is generally deductible.

ww.A vacation trip: A vacation trip is a personal expense, which the IRS does not allow as a business deduction unless it is a legitimate business trip.
ww.A parking fine: Parking fines are penalties for breaking the law and are not deductible, even when incurred while doing business.
ww.Owner's food: Personal meals for the owner are generally personal living costs, not deductible business expenses, apart from limited business meals.

rw: Estimated tax consists of quarterly payments by people, such as self-employed taxpayers, whose income has no or too little tax withheld.

ww.A guess about next year's tax law made b: Estimated tax is paid by the taxpayer, not a forecast of tax law by the revenue agency.
ww.A tax on estimates made by people who fi: Estimated tax is not a tax on guesses; it is a payment of expected income tax made in installments during the year.
ww.A refund from the IRS paid to people who: A refund is money returned for overpaying; estimated tax is a payment made in advance, the reverse of a refund.

rw: Most individual federal returns are due April 15 (or the next business day if it falls on a weekend or holiday).

ww.January 1 each year: January 1 is New Year's Day and the start of the tax year, not the filing deadline for individual returns.
ww.July 4 of each year: July 4 is Independence Day, a federal holiday, and is not the deadline for filing individual tax returns.
ww.December 31 of the year: December 31 ends the tax year for most individuals, but the return for that year is not due until the following April.

rw: Missing the deadline for payroll taxes leads to penalties and interest on the amount owed, because employers hold those taxes in trust for the government.

ww.A discount on the tax owed: Late payment never earns a discount; the IRS adds charges rather than reducing the tax owed.
ww.No consequence at all: Failing to pay payroll taxes has real consequences, including penalties and interest, and serious cases can bring personal liability.
ww.A tax refund check: A refund check comes from overpaying taxes, not from underpaying; an unpaid balance leads to charges instead.

rw: A depreciation deduction lets a business deduct the cost of an asset over its useful life, reflecting wear and tear over time.

ww.A deduction for salaries paid to workers: Salaries are a separate deductible expense; a depreciation deduction covers the cost of using up assets, not wages.
ww.A deduction for interest paid on a loan: Interest paid on loans is a separate deduction; depreciation relates to the wearing out of long-lived property.
ww.A deduction for gifts given to friends a: Gifts to friends and family are personal and not deductible as depreciation; depreciation applies to business assets only.

rw: Using software to examine every payment for duplicates is data analytics, a tool that helps detect fraud and errors faster than manual checks.

ww.Price discrimination by sellers: Price discrimination is a pricing strategy by sellers charging different customers different prices, unrelated to auditing payments.
ww.Manual sampling of a few items by hand: Manual sampling examines a few items by hand; scanning every payment with software is automated and covers the whole population.
ww.Inventory counting by hand weekly: Counting inventory by hand is a physical process; scanning payment records for duplicates uses software to examine transactions.

rw: Recurring invoices automatically bill regular customers on a set schedule, saving time, reducing errors and speeding cash collection.

ww.They remove the need for any customers a: Invoices cannot replace customers; recurring invoices only automate billing for customers who already exist.
ww.They raise prices for the customers who: Recurring invoices repeat the agreed amount on schedule; they do not raise prices unless the business changes the template.
ww.They create duplicate payments to the ve: Recurring invoices bill customers, not vendors; creating duplicate vendor payments would be a control weakness, not a benefit.

rw: Limiting user access prevents unauthorized changes and protects sensitive data, which is a key internal control in accounting software.

ww.To avoid backups of the data kept in the: Backups protect data from loss, so limiting access does not avoid backups; both are controls that protect information.
ww.To slow the system down for all users of: Limiting access has no purpose of slowing the system; permissions work in the background and are meant to protect data.
ww.To increase errors made by the staff in: Restricting user access reduces errors and fraud because only authorized people can change records; it is not intended to increase mistakes.

rw: A payroll specialist calculates employee pay, withholds taxes and deductions, and makes sure paychecks and payroll reports are accurate.

ww.Repairs equipment in the factory and pla: Repairing equipment is the work of a maintenance technician, not a payroll specialist who works with employee pay records.
ww.Sells insurance to individuals and firms: Selling insurance is the work of an insurance agent; payroll specialists handle pay, not policies.
ww.Designs logos and brochures for the mark: Designing logos and brochures is a graphic design and marketing role, not a payroll accounting task.

rw: Financial and budget analysts plan, forecast and analyze budgets, which suits someone who enjoys numbers and projections.

ww.Lifeguard at a large public pool: A lifeguard watches swimmers for safety and does not use budgeting or forecasting skills.
ww.Delivery driver for a courier firm: A delivery driver's work focuses on transporting packages, not on planning or forecasting budgets.
ww.Warehouse loader moving boxes and stock: A warehouse loader moves boxes and stock, which is physical work that does not involve financial planning.

rw: The CMA (Certified Management Accountant) credential is common for management accountants who work with budgeting, cost analysis and decision support.

ww.CPR certificate for giving first aid: A CPR certificate shows first aid training and is unrelated to accounting careers.
ww.CDL license for truck drivers only: A CDL is a commercial driver's license for truck drivers, which has nothing to do with accounting.
ww.EMT license for medical staff only: An EMT license is for emergency medical technicians, a healthcare credential, not a credential for accountants.

rw: The monetary unit assumption says business activity can be measured and recorded in money terms, such as US dollars, which allows amounts to be added.

ww.Currencies of countries may be added wit: Currencies cannot be added without conversion; the monetary unit assumption says to measure in a stable currency, such as the US dollar.
ww.Money is the only thing that matters to: The assumption does not say money is all that matters; it says only that transactions measurable in money are recorded.
ww.Every item must be recorded at its curre: Daily market-price recording is not required; assets are recorded at historical cost under the cost principle, not marked to market each day.

rw: Under the cost principle, assets stay on the books at original purchase price, so the building is carried at $200,000 despite the higher market value.

ww.$260,000: $260,000 is the market value, but the cost principle records assets at original cost, not at changing market values.
ww.$230,000: $230,000 is an invented midpoint; the cost principle uses actual purchase cost, not an average or estimate of value.
ww.$60,000: $60,000 is the unrecorded increase in market value; the cost principle ignores that gain and keeps the asset at its $200,000 purchase price.

rw: In the periodic system, inventory records are updated at the end of the period after a physical count, and cost of goods sold is computed then.

ww.Inventory updates after every sale, so r: Updating inventory after every sale describes the perpetual system; the periodic system updates only after a physical count.
ww.Inventory is never counted by the staff: Under the periodic system, inventory is counted physically, so saying it is never counted is wrong.
ww.Inventory is guessed by the owners from: Inventory under any system must be based on counts or records, not guesses from sales totals.

rw: In rising prices FIFO assigns older, lower costs to cost of goods sold, giving lower COGS and therefore higher net income than LIFO.

ww.Equal: The methods give different results when prices change, so net income is not equal under FIFO and LIFO in a rising-price period.
ww.LIFO: LIFO charges the newest, higher costs to cost of goods sold, which lowers net income during rising prices, so it reports less.
ww.Neither: The two methods do not give the same result when prices change; one reports clearly higher income than the other.

rw: Weighted average divides the total cost of goods available by total units to get an average cost used for both inventory and cost of goods sold.

ww.Ignoring costs when valuing the stock an: Weighted-average costing does not ignore costs; it uses them all, averaging the costs of all units available for sale.
ww.Using the cost of the oldest unit only t: Using the oldest unit's cost is FIFO, not weighted average, which blends all unit costs together.
ww.Using the cost of the latest unit only,: Using the cost of the latest units describes LIFO, not weighted average, which spreads cost across all units.

rw: Assets have a normal debit balance: debits increase them and credits decrease them, matching the left side of the accounting equation.

ww.Liability: Liabilities have a normal credit balance, since they increase with credits and decrease with debits.
ww.Capital: Capital is an equity account with a normal credit balance, increasing when the owner invests or profits are earned.
ww.Revenue: Revenue accounts have a normal credit balance because revenue increases owner's equity, which grows with credits.

rw: Liabilities have a normal credit balance, because they sit on the right side of the accounting equation and increase with credits.

ww.Drawings: Drawings reduce owner's equity, so they have a normal debit balance, not a credit balance.
ww.Expense: Expenses reduce equity, so they carry a normal debit balance and increase with debits.
ww.Asset: Assets sit on the left of the accounting equation and have a normal debit balance, not a credit balance.

rw: Expense accounts have normal debit balances, so a debit increases the expense, such as debiting Rent Expense when rent is paid.

ww.It increases revenue: A debit to an expense account does not touch revenue; it increases the expense itself, as expenses sit on the debit side.
ww.It decreases the expense: Decreasing an expense requires a credit; a debit increases it, because expense accounts have normal debit balances.
ww.It has no effect at all: Every debit has an effect: on an expense account it raises the balance and, with the offsetting credit, records the transaction.

rw: Revenue accounts have normal credit balances, so a credit increases revenue, which in turn increases owner's equity.

ww.It has no effect: A credit always changes the account's balance; for revenue it raises the balance rather than doing nothing.
ww.It increases assets: Revenue does not itself increase assets; a credit to revenue is matched by a debit to cash or receivables, which increases assets.
ww.It decreases revenue: A debit, not a credit, decreases revenue, since revenue accounts normally carry credit balances.

rw: Paying rent increases Rent Expense (debit) and decreases Cash (credit), so the entry is Debit Rent Expense $900, Credit Cash $900.

ww.Debit Rent Expense, credit Payable: Crediting a payable would mean the rent is still owed; the question says $900 was paid in cash, so Cash must be credited.
ww.Debit Prepaid Rent, credit Revenue: Prepaid Rent and Revenue do not apply: paying rent as it comes due is an expense, and paying cash does not create revenue.
ww.Debit Cash, credit Rent Expense: This reverses the entry: debiting Cash would show cash increasing and crediting Rent Expense would reduce an expense, the opposite of paying rent.

rw: Cash comes in (debit Cash) and the service revenue is earned (credit Service Revenue), so Debit Cash $500, Credit Service Revenue $500.

ww.Debit Service Revenue, credit Cash: Debiting Revenue and crediting Cash reverses the entry; receiving cash for services increases both cash and revenue.
ww.Debit Cash, credit Accounts Payable: Accounts Payable is a liability for money owed; services performed for cash earn revenue and do not create a payable.
ww.Debit Accounts Receivable, credit Cash: Debiting Accounts Receivable and crediting Cash would mean the customer owes money and cash goes out, which is not what happened.

rw: An investment increases Cash (debit) and the owner's equity (credit Owner's Capital), so Debit Cash $10,000, Credit Owner's Capital $10,000.

ww.Debit Owner's Capital, credit Cash: This reverses the entry; an owner investment increases cash and capital, rather than reducing them.
ww.Debit Drawings and credit Cash: Drawings record withdrawals by the owner, which reduce equity; an investment is the opposite and increases cash and capital.
ww.Debit Cash and credit the Revenue: An owner investment is not revenue; crediting Revenue would overstate income, while capital is the proper equity account.

rw: Withdrawals reduce owner's equity through the Drawings account (debit) and reduce cash (credit): Debit Owner's Drawings $1,200, Credit Cash $1,200.

ww.Debit Capital and credit Revenue: Capital and revenue are not involved in a personal withdrawal; revenue comes from earning income, not from owner withdrawals.
ww.Debit Salaries Expense, credit Cash: Salaries Expense is for wages paid to employees; an owner's personal withdrawal is recorded as drawings, not as an expense.
ww.Debit Cash and credit the Drawings: Debiting Cash and crediting Drawings reverses the entry; a withdrawal takes cash out of the business.

rw: The unpaid portion is $5,000 - $2,000 = $3,000, which is credited to Accounts Payable, with $2,000 credited to Cash and $5,000 debited to Equipment.

ww.$5,000: $5,000 is the whole cost of the equipment; part was paid in cash, so only the unpaid portion goes to Accounts Payable.
ww.$7,000: $7,000 adds the cash payment to the cost, which makes no sense; the payable cannot exceed the $5,000 purchase price.
ww.$2,000: $2,000 is the cash paid, which is credited to Cash; the payable covers the rest of the cost.

rw: A trial balance lists all ledger account balances to verify that total debits equal total credits, which checks the mathematical accuracy of posting.

ww.To list the customers and their details: A list of customers and details is a customer or receivables ledger, not a trial balance, which lists account balances.
ww.To show the net income for the whole yea: Net income is shown on the income statement, not the trial balance, although the trial balance helps prepare it.
ww.To prove the ledger has no errors in it: A trial balance cannot prove there are no errors, because errors like wrong accounts or omitted entries keep debits and credits equal.

rw: Yes: posting the right amount to the wrong account, or omitting a whole transaction, leaves debits equal to credits even though errors exist.

ww.Only for assets, never for any other typ: Errors that leave a trial balance in balance can occur in any account type, not just assets.
ww.Only for expenses, never for any other t: Errors that leave a trial balance in balance can occur in any account type, not just expenses.
ww.No, never, because debits always equal c: Equal debits and credits only prove mathematical equality; they do not prove the entries are correct, so a balanced trial balance may hide errors.

rw: Debits exceeding credits by $1,500 suggests a $1,500 error, such as an omitted credit, a one-sided entry or a posting mistake.

ww.Taxes are due on the $1,500 gap between: Taxes due are unrelated to a trial balance difference; the $1,500 gap signals a bookkeeping error rather than a tax issue.
ww.The business earned $1,500, as debits ex: A business earning money does not cause debits to exceed credits in the trial balance; double-entry always records equal amounts.
ww.Nothing is wrong, as the two totals are: A trial balance must balance exactly; even a small difference signals an error that must be found, however close the totals look.

rw: A transposition error is reversing digits in a number, such as writing 54 as 45, which makes a difference divisible by 9.

ww.Adding the numbers wrongly in a column o: Adding numbers wrongly is a mathematical or addition error; a transposition error specifically reverses digits.
ww.Posting to the wrong account, such as th: Posting to a wrong account is an error of principle or commission; it differs from reversing the digits of a number.
ww.Omitting an entry from the books by mist: Leaving out an entry is an error of omission, not a transposition of digits.

rw: A difference divisible by 9, such as $36, strongly suggests digits were reversed, like writing 54 as 45 (a $9 difference per swap), which is a transposition error.

ww.A change in tax laws: Changes in tax laws do not affect whether debits and credits equal; they do not explain a small trial balance difference.
ww.A depreciation change: A change in depreciation method affects expense amounts but is recorded with equal debits and credits, so it would not cause a trial balance difference.
ww.A missing sales entry: A missing sales entry omits both debit and credit, so the trial balance would still balance; it would not create a $36 difference.

rw: Accumulated Depreciation is a contra-asset account, so it has a normal credit balance, which reduces the related asset's book value.

ww.Debit: A debit balance is normal for assets; accumulated depreciation is a contra-asset with the opposite, credit, balance.
ww.Zero: Accumulated Depreciation grows each period as depreciation is recorded, so it normally carries a balance rather than zero.
ww.Either: Every account has a normal balance; accumulated depreciation normally carries a credit balance, not either one.

rw: Sales Returns and Allowances is a contra-revenue account, so it has a normal debit balance that reduces gross sales to net sales.

ww.Either: Every account has a normal side; Sales Returns and Allowances is a contra-revenue account with a normal debit balance, not either.
ww.Credit: A credit balance is normal for revenue, but this is a contra-revenue account, so it carries the opposite, debit, balance.
ww.Zero: It builds up as customers return goods or receive allowances, so it normally has a balance and is not zero.

rw: The matching principle records expenses in the same period as the revenues they help earn, so profit is measured accurately for the period.

ww.Debits match credits in every entry that: Debits matching credits is double-entry bookkeeping, not the matching principle, which concerns timing of expenses.
ww.Revenue is recorded when cash is receive: Recording revenue when cash is received describes cash-basis accounting, which differs from the matching principle.
ww.Assets match liabilities in total on the: Assets equaling liabilities plus equity is the accounting equation, not the matching principle, which links expenses to revenues.

rw: The cost principle records assets at their original purchase cost, which is objective and verifiable, and keeps them at that cost despite market changes.

ww.Assets are recorded at market value each: Recording assets at market value each year contradicts the cost principle, which keeps them at original cost.
ww.Assets are not recorded in the books of: Assets are recorded in the books; the cost principle just says how they are valued.
ww.Assets are recorded at replacement cost: Replacement cost is a different valuation approach; the cost principle uses what was actually paid when the asset was acquired.

rw: The monetary unit concept says only transactions that can be measured in money terms are recorded in the accounting records.

ww.Employee morale is recorded in the books: Employee morale cannot be measured in money, so the monetary unit concept excludes it from the books.
ww.All events are recorded in the books of: Not all events are recorded; the monetary unit concept limits records to events measurable in money.
ww.Customer opinions are recorded as soon a: Customer opinions cannot be reliably measured in money, so the monetary unit concept leaves them out.

rw: The revenue recognition principle records revenue when it is earned, usually when goods or services are delivered, not necessarily when cash arrives.

ww.Revenue is never recorded in the books u: Revenue is recorded as it is earned during operations, not only when the firm closes down.
ww.Revenue is recorded when cash is paid, w: Revenue is recognized when earned, not when cash is paid; the payment date does not decide timing.
ww.Revenue is recorded at year end only, wh: Revenue is recorded throughout the year as earned, not just at year end when books are closed.

rw: Cash-basis accounting records revenue only when cash is received and expenses only when cash is paid, regardless of when they were earned or incurred.

ww.Recording revenue when earned and expens: Recording revenue when earned and expenses when incurred describes accrual accounting, the opposite of the cash basis.
ww.Recording only the credits from every en: Recording only the credits of an entry is not an accounting method; double-entry records both debits and credits.
ww.Recording estimates of revenue and expen: Recording estimates before events take place is not cash basis; it involves anticipating transactions rather than actual cash flow.

rw: Under accrual accounting, revenue is recorded when earned, so December is correct since the job was completed then; the January payment just collects a receivable.

ww.Both months: Revenue is recorded once, when earned, not in both months; counting it twice would overstate revenue.
ww.Neither: The job was completed, so the revenue is earned and must be recorded in some period, not skipped.
ww.January: January is when cash is received, which is the cash basis; accrual accounting records revenue when earned.

rw: Under accrual accounting, the expense is recorded when incurred; December's electricity was used in December, so the bill is accrued as an expense then.

ww.Both months: The expense is recorded once, in the period it was incurred, not in two months.
ww.January: January is when the bill is received or paid, which reflects cash-basis timing; accrual records the expense in December.
ww.Neither: The electricity was used, so an expense exists and must be recorded in some period.

rw: A check stub records details of a check, such as date, payee and amount, for later reference in reconciling the account.

ww.Closing the books at the end of the fisc: Closing the books is done with closing entries, not with a check stub.
ww.Opening an account at a local bank for t: Opening a bank account uses signature cards and deposit forms, not check stubs.
ww.Paying employees only, with the stub han: Check stubs are not limited to paying employees; they record details of any check issued by the firm.

rw: Owner's equity equals assets minus liabilities, the residual claim of the owner after creditors are paid.

ww.Liabilities minus assets: Liabilities minus assets reverses the formula, which would produce a negative amount for a solvent business.
ww.Assets plus liabilities: Assets plus liabilities double counts; the accounting equation sets assets equal to liabilities plus owner's equity.
ww.Revenue minus assets: Revenue minus assets mixes an income statement item with a balance sheet item and has no meaning as an equity formula.

rw: Liabilities = assets - owner's equity = $80,000 - $50,000 = $30,000, from the equation assets = liabilities + equity.

ww.$50,000: $50,000 is the owner's equity, not liabilities; liabilities are assets minus equity.
ww.$130,000: $130,000 adds equity to assets, but the equation requires subtracting: assets = liabilities + equity.
ww.$80,000: $80,000 is the total of assets; liabilities are only the part not funded by the owner.

rw: Assets = liabilities + owner's equity = $25,000 + $40,000 = $65,000, since the equation requires both sides to be equal.

ww.$25,000: $25,000 is only the liabilities; total assets include the owner's equity funding as well.
ww.$15,000: $15,000 subtracts equity from liabilities, but the equation adds them to get assets.
ww.$40,000: $40,000 is only the owner's equity; total assets equal liabilities plus equity.

rw: Paying $600 reduces Cash (an asset) and reduces Accounts Payable (a liability) by the same amount, leaving equity unchanged.

ww.Increases assets and liabilities by the: Paying a payable does not increase assets; cash goes out, so assets fall as liabilities fall.
ww.Decreases equity by the same amount paid: Paying a payable that was already recorded does not reduce equity; the expense was recognized earlier, and only cash and liabilities change.
ww.Increases assets only, by the amount pai: Paying a debt does not increase assets; cash decreases, and the liability also decreases.

rw: Supplies (an asset) increase, and Accounts Payable (a liability) increases by the same amount, so the equation stays balanced.

ww.Decreases assets by the cost of supplies: Buying supplies on account increases assets (supplies) rather than decreasing them; cash is not paid yet.
ww.Increases equity by the cost of supplies: Buying on credit does not change equity; the asset rises and an equal liability is recorded.
ww.Decreases liabilities as supplies get pa: Liabilities increase when supplies are bought on account, and they decrease only when the bill is later paid.

rw: A credit sale raises Accounts Receivable (an asset) and Service Revenue, which increases owner's equity, so both sides rise equally.

ww.Increases liabilities and decreases owne: Earning revenue on credit increases assets (receivables) and increases equity, not liabilities.
ww.Decreases assets by the full amount earn: Assets increase because a receivable is created, so decreasing them is wrong.
ww.Decreases equity by the full amount earn: Revenue increases owner's equity; it does not reduce it.

rw: Paying wages in cash reduces Cash (an asset) and raises Wages Expense, which reduces owner's equity.

ww.No effect on assets or on owner's equity: Paying wages does affect the books: cash goes out and an expense reduces equity.
ww.Increases assets by the total amount of: Paying wages reduces cash, so assets decrease rather than increase.
ww.Increases liabilities and increases owne: Paying wages does not create a liability or add to equity; cash is paid out and an expense reduces equity.

rw: The accounting cycle begins by analyzing transactions from source documents such as invoices and receipts, and then they are journalized.

ww.Prepare financial statements for the own: Preparing financial statements comes late in the cycle, after the ledger, trial balance and adjustments are done.
ww.Close the books at the end of the year: Closing the books comes near the end of the cycle, after statements are prepared.
ww.Post to the ledger accounts of the firm: Posting to the ledger follows journalizing, so it cannot be the first step.

rw: After transactions are journalized, they are posted to the ledger accounts, which sorts the information by account.

ww.Financial statements: Financial statements come near the end of the cycle, after posting, trial balance and adjusting entries.
ww.Adjusting entries: Adjusting entries come after the trial balance is prepared, not immediately after journalizing.
ww.Closing the entries: Closing entries come near the end of the cycle, after statements are prepared.

rw: The worksheet organizes trial balance data, adjustments and balances to help prepare the financial statements.

ww.To replace the ledger accounts of the fi: The worksheet is a working tool and does not replace the ledger accounts, which remain the permanent records.
ww.To pay bills owed by the firm to its sup: Bills are paid through payment procedures, not the worksheet, which is only an analysis tool.
ww.To record source documents such as invoi: Source documents such as invoices are the starting records of transactions, not the worksheet, which is prepared later.

rw: Adjusting entries made at period end update accounts for accruals and deferrals so revenues and expenses are in the correct period.

ww.Entries for budgets that managers prepar: Budgets for next year are planning tools, not adjusting entries, which update accounts at period end.
ww.Entries for new customers who sign up wi: New customers are handled through sales and credit procedures, not by adjusting entries.
ww.Entries that correct spelling mistakes i: Correcting customer names is a data cleanup; adjusting entries are accounting entries tied to timing of revenues and expenses.

rw: Supplies used = $2,000 - $1,200 = $800, so debit Supplies Expense $800 and credit Supplies $800 to reduce the asset to the $1,200 on hand.

ww.Debit Cash $800 and credit Supplies for: Cash is not involved in this adjustment since the supplies were already paid for; the entry moves cost from asset to expense.
ww.Debit Supplies $800, credit Expense for: This entry is reversed and vague: the asset is reduced by a credit to Supplies and the expense is increased by a debit.
ww.No entry is needed for the supplies used: An entry is needed; without it, assets would be overstated and expenses understated by the $800 of supplies used.

rw: Monthly insurance expense = $3,600 / 12 months = $300, which is moved from Prepaid Insurance to expense each month.

ww.$30: $30 would be a monthly figure for a tiny policy, but $3,600 over 12 months is $300 per month.
ww.$1,200: $1,200 is the cost for four months, not one; spread across 12 months the cost is much smaller.
ww.$3,600: $3,600 is the total premium for the whole year, not the monthly expense.

rw: After 3 months $900 has expired ($300 x 3), so Prepaid Insurance = $3,600 - $900 = $2,700 for the remaining 9 months.

ww.$300: $300 is the monthly expense, not the balance; after 3 months the unexpired portion is much larger.
ww.$900: $900 is the expense used after 3 months, not the remaining balance of prepaid insurance.
ww.$3,600: $3,600 is the original premium; after 3 months some has expired, so the balance is lower.

rw: Unpaid but earned wages require Debit Wages Expense $2,000 and Credit Wages Payable $2,000, matching the expense to the period it was incurred.

ww.Debit Cash and credit Wages Expense $2,0: Cash is not paid yet, so crediting Cash would be wrong; the wages are owed, not paid.
ww.Debit Wages Payable, credit Wages Expens: Debiting Wages Payable and crediting Wages Expense reverses the entry and would reduce a liability and expense instead of recording them.
ww.No entry is needed for the unpaid wages: An entry is required; skipping it would understate expenses and liabilities, violating the matching principle.

rw: Accrued interest earned but not received requires Debit Interest Receivable $1,500 and Credit Interest Revenue $1,500, so income is reported in the right period.

ww.Debit Interest Revenue $1,500, credit Re: Interest Revenue should be credited, not debited, and the debit should be to a receivable; this wording reverses the entry.
ww.No entry is needed until the cash is rec: Under accrual accounting, earned revenue must be recorded in the period earned, even without cash.
ww.Debit Cash and credit Interest Revenue $: Cash has not been received, so debiting Cash would be wrong; a receivable should be recorded instead.
